content: Litmus is a water-soluble mixture of various dyes that are extracted from lichens, particularly from the species Roccella tinctoria. This mixture is identified by the CAS number 1393-92-6. It is commonly absorbed onto filter paper, which then becomes a pH indicator. This indicator is one of the oldest tools used to test the acidity or alkalinity of materials. At a temperature of 25°C, neutral litmus paper appears purple in color. The litmus mixture itself contains approximately 10 to 15 different dyes, including erythrolein (or erythrolitmin), azolitmin, spaniolitmin, leucorcein, and leucazolitmin. Pure azolitmin exhibits nearly the same pH-indicating properties as the litmus mixture. The use of litmus dates back to around 1300 AD, when it was first employed by the Spanish alchemist Arnaldus de Villa Nova. By the 16th century, the blue dye component of litmus was being extracted from certain lichens, particularly in the Netherlands. Litmus is derived from various species of lichens. Historically, the dyes were extracted from species such as Roccella tinctoria (found in South America), Roccella fuciformis (from Angola and Madagascar), Roccella pygmaea (from Algeria), Roccella phycopsis, Lecanora tartarea (from Norway and Sweden), Variolaria dealbata, Ochrolechia parella, Parmotrema tinctorum, and Parmelia. In modern times, the primary sources of litmus are Roccella montagnei (from Mozambique) and Dendrographa leucophoea (from California). The primary application of litmus is to determine whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. Wet litmus paper can also be used to test water-soluble gases. When a gas dissolves in water, the resulting solution can cause a color change in the litmus paper. For example, chlorine gas turns blue litmus paper white due to a bleaching reaction. This reaction is irreversible, meaning that in this case, litmus does not function as a pH indicator. To test whether a substance is neutral, both blue and red litmus papers are required. If the substance is neutral, the color of the litmus paper will either remain unchanged or turn purple on both types of paper.
